scenes.visual: Title card 'Reading Selection in Genes'. COLOUR MAP, the same in both films: GOLD = a DNA change (a new mutation, a tick mark, a changed site); BLUE = branch and dots of species A; GREEN = branch and dots of species B; GREY = the common ancestor and unchanged sites; a brown stone icon = a fossil; CORAL = amino-acid (nonsynonymous) changes and the dN counter; TEAL = the dS counter. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Dots, trees, codon blocks and beads are simple cartoons; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. No molecular structures.

scenes.tts: Where selection acts, changes depart from the neutral count. Purifying selection can make them lag; positive selection can make them run ahead. So how could you catch that in a real gene?
scenes.visual: The Y tree with GOLD ticks on BLUE and GREEN branches, label 'neutral count'. Beside it, two schematic tick tracks against a dashed 'neutral count' line: on one, a few ticks are crossed out in red ('purifying: lags'), so it falls behind; on the other, extra CORAL ticks land ('positive: runs ahead'). Both labelled 'possible clues, not proof'. A magnifying glass hovers with a question mark: 'selection?'.
scenes.narration: Where selection acts, changes depart from the neutral count. Purifying selection can make them lag; positive selection can make them run ahead. So how could you catch that in a real gene?

scenes.tts: Here is the trick. Find two kinds of change in the same gene that neutrality says should behave alike. If they part ways by more than chance allows, selection may be at work.
scenes.visual: Two tick tracks side by side, one CORAL and one TEAL, running at the same average pace with small random wobbles; then the CORAL one slows well beyond the wobble and the tracks drift apart. Labels 'neutral: same average pace' then 'departure beyond chance = clue to selection'.
scenes.narration: Here is the trick. Find two kinds of change in the same gene that neutrality says should behave alike. If they part ways by more than chance allows, selection may be at work.

scenes.tts: Take a coding gene, read three letters at a time. The genetic code has several codons for most amino acids. So some changes keep the amino acid. These are synonymous.
scenes.visual: A row of six codon blocks, each three small GREY squares, above a string of six coloured beads (amino acids). One square in the third block turns GOLD; its bead keeps its colour. Label 'synonymous: same amino acid'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Take a coding gene, read three letters at a time. The genetic code has several codons for most amino acids. So some changes keep the amino acid. These are synonymous.

scenes.tts: Other changes alter the amino acid. These are nonsynonymous, or replacement, changes. If synonymous changes are neutral, they are a built-in control for the replacements.
scenes.visual: A square in the fifth block turns GOLD and its bead flips to CORAL. Label 'nonsynonymous (replacement): new amino acid'. A TEAL bracket over the synonymous change reads 'control'.
scenes.narration: Other changes alter the amino acid. These are nonsynonymous, or replacement, changes. If synonymous changes are neutral, they are a built-in control for the replacements.

scenes.tts: Count each kind along a branch, per site where it could happen. Call them d N and d S. Their ratio is called omega.
scenes.caption: Count each kind along a branch, per site where it could happen. Call them dN and dS. Their ratio is called omega.
scenes.visual: Two counters on a branch: CORAL 'dN' and TEAL 'dS', both ticking upward. Below them a semicircular dial labelled 'omega = dN / dS' with marks at 0, 1 and 2+.
scenes.narration: Count each kind along a branch, per site where it could happen. Call them dN and dS. Their ratio is called omega.

scenes.tts: Below one, replacements were fixed more slowly than silent changes. That suggests purifying selection removed some. Near one is consistent with neutrality. Above one suggests positive selection.
scenes.visual: Three runs of the counters, one after another. Run 1: CORAL lags far behind TEAL; dial needle below 1, label 'purifying selection suggested'. Run 2: they keep pace; needle at 1, label 'consistent with neutrality'. Run 3: CORAL races ahead; needle above 1, label 'positive selection suggested'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Below one, replacements were fixed more slowly than silent changes. That suggests purifying selection removed some. Near one is consistent with neutrality. Above one suggests positive selection.

scenes.tts: A second test uses variation inside a species. In nineteen ninety-one, John McDonald and Martin Kreitman applied it to the A D H gene of fruit flies. The gene makes alcohol dehydrogenase.
scenes.caption: A second test uses variation inside a species. In 1991, John McDonald and Martin Kreitman applied it to the Adh gene of fruit flies. The gene makes alcohol dehydrogenase.
scenes.visual: Name card 'McDonald & Kreitman, Nature, 1991'. A cartoon fruit fly beside a gene bar labelled 'Adh (alcohol dehydrogenase)'; three fly icons labelled 'three Drosophila species'.
scenes.narration: A second test uses variation inside a species. In 1991, John McDonald and Martin Kreitman applied it to the Adh gene of fruit flies. The gene makes alcohol dehydrogenase.

scenes.tts: Sort every change into a table. The columns are replacement and synonymous. One row holds variants within a species. The other holds differences fixed between species.
scenes.visual: An empty 2 x 2 table builds: columns 'replacement' (CORAL header) and 'synonymous' (TEAL header); rows 'varies within a species' and 'fixed between species'.
scenes.narration: Sort every change into a table. The columns are replacement and synonymous. One row holds variants within a species. The other holds differences fixed between species.

scenes.tts: Under neutrality, a variant within a species is a passing stage, on its way to fixation or loss. So both rows should hold the same ratio of replacement to synonymous changes.
scenes.visual: A GOLD variant dot inside a population box drifts up to fill the box (fixed) or fades out (lost); arrows from the 'varies' row to the 'fixed' row. A '=' sign appears between the two rows' ratios, label 'neutral expectation: same ratio'.
scenes.narration: Under neutrality, a variant within a species is a passing stage, on its way to fixation or loss. So both rows should hold the same ratio of replacement to synonymous changes.

scenes.tts: The variants row fills first, and it is mostly synonymous. If replacements were neutral, what should the fixed row look like?
scenes.visual: Polymorphism row fills with counts on screen only (McDonald & Kreitman 1991, Table 2): replacement 2, synonymous 42. The fixed row stays empty with a question mark.
scenes.narration: The variants row fills first, and it is mostly synonymous. If replacements were neutral, what should the fixed row look like?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: what ratio in the fixed row?'.

scenes.tts: Neutrality predicts the same ratio. Instead, the fixed row held more replacements than the variants predicted. McDonald and Kreitman suggested this reflected adaptive fixation.
scenes.visual: A ghost row shows the predicted fixed counts at the variants' ratio. Then the real fixed row fills (on screen only; McDonald & Kreitman 1991, Table 2): replacement 7, synonymous 17. The replacement cell glows CORAL; on-screen ratio comparison '7/17 against 2/42' with label 'excess fixed replacements'.
scenes.narration: Neutrality predicts the same ratio. Instead, the fixed row held more replacements than the variants predicted. McDonald and Kreitman suggested this reflected adaptive fixation.

scenes.tts: Here each kind of change is the control for the other. So this test needs no clock and no dated split.
scenes.visual: The table's TEAL column and CORAL column each point an arrow at the other, label 'each is the other's control'. The fossil stone icon and a clock icon are crossed out.
scenes.narration: Here each kind of change is the control for the other. So this test needs no clock and no dated split.

scenes.tts: Both tests are model inferences, and each model can fail. A signal like this still needs further checks before it counts as adaptation.
scenes.visual: A stamp 'statistical signal' lands on the table, then a checklist slides in beside it with empty boxes: 'alignment', 'orthology', 'mutation model', 'synonymous sites neutral?', 'function test'.
scenes.narration: Both tests are model inferences, and each model can fail. A signal like this still needs further checks before it counts as adaptation.

scenes.tts: Both tests ask the same question. Did one kind of change keep pace with the neutral count? A departure is a clue to selection, not proof.
scenes.visual: The two tick tracks from the opening, TEAL steady and CORAL parting from it, under the Y tree from the first film.
scenes.narration: Both tests ask the same question. Did one kind of change keep pace with the neutral count? A departure is a clue to selection, not proof.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot. Line: 'A departure from the neutral count is a clue to selection.'
